papers.headline: Why colder transistors do not always switch more sharply
papers.summary: Cooling should make a transistor's turn-on sharper, yet real devices show peaks, valleys and saturation. A transport-based scaling theory separates the effects of band-tail states from the measurement conditions that shape these anomalies.
papers.takeaway: A low-temperature switching plateau is not always an intrinsic device limit.
papers.question: Why does subthreshold swing, a measure of how sharply a transistor turns on, stop following the ideal temperature dependence in ultrathin-body MOSFETs? Similar anomalies appear in silicon, two-dimensional and oxide-semiconductor devices, but not every plateau has the same physical origin.
papers.approach: The study uses a diffusive Landauer transport formulation coupled to the transistor's electrostatics. Numerical calculations and asymptotic analysis distinguish localized band-tail states, which store charge, from conductive tail states, which also carry current. The analysis yields compact scaling expressions and compares them with published silicon measurements.
findings: For localized tail states, the competition between tail-state charge and gate control can generate a peak-and-valley temperature dependence. Its onset is approximately governed by the ratio of tail-state capacitance to oxide capacitance.

In the localized-tail model, a deep-cryogenic plateau depends on the reference current and scattering model. Lowering the reference current lowers this measurement-related floor; it should not automatically be interpreted as an intrinsic switching limit.
Temperature scales in the theory separate the band-tail energy width from the onset of carrier degeneracy, providing a route to extract defect-related parameters from electrical measurements.
papers.significance: The work connects an unusual electrical signature to the microscopic states and measurement choices behind it. This can help researchers interpret cryogenic transistor data and distinguish material-quality changes from the conditions used to measure switching.
papers.scope: This is a transport-theory study, not a demonstration of a newly fabricated transistor or quantum-computing circuit. Conclusions about the current-dependent floor apply to the localized-tail model; conductive tail states have different saturation behavior.
papers.source_note: Full text: author's accepted manuscript stored in Zotero. Journal citation is taken from the bibliography.

papers.headline: Bringing thermal and stress analysis to chip scale
papers.summary: A chip is too large for many neural simulation models to handle at once. FP-DDM solves overlapping regions with a reusable model, then uses physics and interface matching to assemble a consistent large-domain solution.
papers.takeaway: Local neural solvers become more useful when their boundaries obey global physics.
papers.question: How can neural simulation support chip-scale thermal and mechanical analysis without requiring the entire problem to fit on a GPU? Dividing the chip into small regions helps with memory, but the local solutions must still agree across their boundaries.
papers.approach: FP-DDM combines a shared Fourier neural operator with overlapping domain decomposition. Test-time physics adaptation refines predictions using governing equations, while Neural Schwarz Acceleration directly optimizes interface boundary values. CPU-GPU offloading streams subdomains instead of keeping the complete domain in GPU memory.
findings: In the reported comparisons, gradient-guided interface updates converge faster than classical boundary exchange; a coarse homogenized starting field further improves convergence.
Physics-based test-time adaptation transfers pretrained models to stress problems and previously unseen layout-derived material fields without ground-truth labels during adaptation.
The implementation supports problems of up to 10 billion cells through CPU-GPU offloading. A separate layout-density example demonstrates gradient-based temperature optimization.
papers.significance: The framework links simulation with design: material distributions, physical response and design objectives can be connected in one differentiable workflow. It offers a route toward thermal-stress-aware semiconductor system and layout co-optimization.
papers.scope: The demonstrations concern steady-state thermal conduction and thermoelastic problems. The 10-billion-cell result establishes executable scale, not benchmarked accuracy for every cell at that scale. The layout optimization uses a simplified metal-density-to-conductivity mapping, not a complete production design-rule flow.
papers.source_note: Full text: seven-page DAC 2026 paper stored in Zotero. The DOI is printed in the paper.

papers.headline: Two routes to controlling oxygen vacancies
papers.summary: Mechanical strain and thermal annealing can push oxide-semiconductor defects in different directions. Atomistic calculations show why local bonding and structural relaxation, rather than density alone, determine whether vacancy-related electrons remain trapped or become mobile.
papers.takeaway: Local atomic arrangements matter more than a simple densification picture.
papers.question: Why can compressive strain and thermal annealing produce opposite electrical trends in amorphous oxide semiconductors, even when both are associated with a denser material? The answer matters because oxygen vacancies can behave as electron-trapping states or electron donors.
papers.approach: The study combines density functional theory, configuration-coordinate analysis and ab initio molecular dynamics for oxygen vacancies in amorphous IGZO. Fixed-volume annealing simulations separate structural relaxation from a change in overall density, allowing the authors to examine the role of specific interatomic distances.
findings: Shorter key metal-metal distances favor localized, bonding-like vacancy states; increasing those distances can shift defect levels toward the conduction band and promote donor-like behavior.
Annealing can relax the atomic network and increase critical local distances even without changing the cell volume. This distinguishes its effect from simple mechanical compression.
The results connect defect-state changes to threshold-voltage shifts, while also showing that localized and delocalized states can coexist after annealing.
papers.significance: The mechanism provides a physical basis for choosing strain and thermal-processing strategies in oxide electronics. It connects atomic-scale defect engineering to the device-level goals of controlling threshold voltage, switching behavior and reliability.
papers.scope: The calculations establish mechanism-level trends using a limited set of oxygen-vacancy configurations in IGZO. They are not a statistically complete model of all defects formed during fabrication, nor a guarantee that annealing delocalizes every vacancy.
papers.source_note: Full text: published Chemistry of Materials article stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: Learning the structure behind changing dynamics
papers.summary: A model can fit observed trajectories yet miss the system's underlying structure. Adversarial orthogonality helps distinguish a change of coordinates from a genuine change in dynamics.
papers.takeaway: Good predictions should preserve meaningful dynamical structure, not just short trajectories.
papers.question: How can a learned dynamical model adapt when its starting model has the wrong qualitative behavior, without mixing up coordinate changes and real physical changes?
papers.approach: The framework jointly learns a smooth invertible transformation and low-dimensional adjustments to source dynamics. An adversarial orthogonality constraint separates adjustments from changes that a coordinate transformation could already explain.
findings: The method separates coordinate-dependent variation from intrinsic changes in the dynamics.
Benchmarks recover canonical structures including bifurcations, symmetries and invariant sets more faithfully than the reported baselines.
papers.significance: This offers a route to scientific models that remain interpretable when observations are limited and a system changes regime.
papers.scope: The evidence comes from dynamical-system benchmarks. It is not a demonstration of a complete semiconductor manufacturing model; extensions to more complex and higher-dimensional corrections remain open.
papers.source_note: Full text: ICML 2026 paper stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: How thin is too thin for a transistor channel?
papers.summary: Thinner channels improve gate control, but roughness can sharply reduce carrier mobility. A scaling framework connects this mobility cliff to confinement and a critical channel thickness.
papers.takeaway: Channel thickness uniformity becomes critical near the mobility cliff.
papers.question: Can the mobility loss in very thin channels be described across different semiconductor technologies with a common physical framework?
papers.approach: The study decomposes measured long-channel mobility into scattering contributions, then accounts for finite potential barriers and wavefunction penetration to explain thickness-dependent scaling.
findings: Finite confinement helps explain why the roughness-related thickness exponent differs from the ideal infinite-well prediction.
A compact analytical model extracts a critical thickness and its associated mobility trade-off from thickness-dependent data.
papers.significance: The framework connects interface quality and process control to the scaling choices made for future thin-body transistors.
papers.scope: This is a long-channel mobility scaling analysis across reported technologies. It does not establish a complete short-channel CFET design rule or eliminate other sources of variability.
papers.source_note: Full text: IEEE EDL article stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: Making simulation AI recognize the same physics
papers.summary: Two inputs can look very different to a neural model while describing equivalent physics. Dimensionless test-time projection brings those inputs closer to familiar examples without retraining the model.
papers.takeaway: A change in physical scale need not be a change in the underlying physics.
papers.question: How can a pretrained simulation surrogate remain useful when input units, magnitudes and physical scales shift beyond its training examples?
papers.approach: Buckingham π-invariants constrain a log-space input projection toward the training distribution. Cluster representatives reduce the cost of finding suitable reference inputs.
findings: The projection improves out-of-distribution predictions in the reported thermal-conduction and linear-elasticity benchmarks without updating model weights.
Clustering reduces projection cost while retaining much of the accuracy benefit of comparing with every training sample.
papers.significance: The work connects dimensional analysis with reusable AI tools for thermal and stress simulation.
papers.scope: The method assumes appropriate governing invariants. Highly irregular fields, empirical components and shifts outside the trained invariant range can still limit performance.
papers.source_note: Full text: ICLR 2026 paper stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: Controlling atomic stacking across a wafer
papers.summary: The stacking order of two boron nitride layers changes their functionality. Step-edge-guided growth produces uniform Bernal-stacked bilayers and integrates them into two-dimensional transistor arrays.
papers.takeaway: Atomic stacking can be engineered as a wafer-scale process variable.
papers.question: How can a metastable, functional stacking arrangement be grown uniformly rather than obtained only in isolated two-dimensional flakes?
papers.approach: Flow-modulated metal-organic chemical vapor deposition is combined with monoatomic nickel step edges. Atomic-resolution characterization and first-principles calculations connect growth conditions to stacking selection.
findings: The reported growth route favors self-limited Bernal-stacked bilayers on nickel/sapphire substrates.
The films function as thin dielectric interlayers in MoS2 transistors, with polarization-linked nonvolatile switching demonstrated.
papers.significance: The study links crystal growth, interface engineering and functional device integration.
papers.scope: The demonstrated material/substrate combination and transistor arrays do not establish a production-ready process for all wafer sizes or a qualified commercial memory technology.
papers.source_note: Full text: Small article stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: What happens when oxide transistors get hot?
papers.summary: IGZO transistors show an unusual mobility increase at elevated temperatures. Measurements and transport modeling separate the resilience of the channel from degradation in the gate dielectric.
papers.takeaway: A stable channel does not automatically mean a stable complete transistor stack.
papers.question: How well can an oxide-semiconductor channel withstand high temperatures, and why can its measured mobility increase rather than decrease?
papers.approach: ALD-grown IGZO FETs are measured in situ up to 750 °C. Scattering-based mobility modeling and atomistic information are used to interpret the temperature-dependent transport.
findings: The study reports increased field-effect mobility at intermediate high temperatures, consistent with reduced grain-boundary scattering.
Channel performance remains relatively stable in the reported 600 °C hold, while gate-dielectric degradation becomes an important limitation at higher temperatures.
papers.significance: Separating channel and dielectric behavior helps evaluate materials for demanding thermal budgets and extreme-environment electronics.
papers.scope: Specific devices and test durations were studied. Operation up to 750 °C is not equivalent to reliable long-term switching at that temperature or qualification for a finished product.
papers.source_note: Full text: IEEE EDL article stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: Reading hidden defects with an electrical pulse
papers.summary: Single-pulse charge pumping probes traps in ultrathin oxide transistors without optical access. Electrical measurements and atomistic calculations connect the extracted signals to defect-related states.
papers.takeaway: Fast electrical metrology can connect process changes with microscopic defect physics.
papers.question: How can interface traps and subgap states be characterized in thin or buried channels where conventional optical measurements are difficult?
papers.approach: The collaboration combines single-pulse charge pumping, a reliability model and hybrid-DFT calculations for oxide TFTs. Our group's contribution includes the first-principles modeling used to interpret defect states.
findings: The pulse-based measurements extract repeatable interface-trap information and improve threshold-shift predictions when included in the reported reliability model.
Annealing-related subgap-state changes are interpreted through band-tail and oxygen-vacancy contributions.
papers.significance: The work links electrical characterization, process optimization and atomistic defect understanding.
papers.scope: The demonstration uses specific In2O3 and IGZO devices. Broader applicability to other thin-body architectures remains a proposed extension rather than a universal validation.
papers.source_note: Full text: IRPS 2026 paper stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: Following the ions that change a memory's state
papers.summary: An independently contacted double-layer ECRAM lets researchers measure both active layers during switching. Their reciprocal response offers insight into how oxygen vacancies move.
papers.takeaway: Observing both sides of the device reveals more than a single conductance trace.
papers.question: How can the movement of oxygen vacancies be tracked during electrochemical memory operation without relying only on destructive post-measurement analysis?
papers.approach: IRIS-ECRAM uses separately contacted tungsten-oxide layers to measure conductance changes on both sides of an electrolyte during switching.
findings: The two layers show reciprocal potentiation and depression, linking their electrical response to electrochemical ion motion.
The experiments identify a temporary-reservoir role for the electrolyte and include a small-array demonstration.
papers.significance: Understanding ion pathways can guide the structure and operating conditions of analog memory devices for in-memory computing.
papers.scope: The paper includes a 2 × 2 array; this is not evidence of large-scale, production-ready integration. More complex ECRAM systems and larger arrays require further validation.
papers.source_note: Full text: Small article stored in Zotero. The library records the publication year but not the month.

papers.headline: Why a 2D material ages differently on different surfaces
papers.summary: A neighboring layer can change how MoTe2 reacts with air. Controlled exposures and first-principles calculations connect interface charge redistribution with oxidation pathways.
papers.takeaway: The supporting interface is part of a material's reliability strategy.
papers.question: Why does the same air-sensitive semiconductor degrade differently when it contacts a metal rather than an insulating layer?
papers.approach: The collaboration studies MoTe2 heterointerfaces under ambient and controlled oxygen/moisture exposure, supported by first-principles analysis of electronic redistribution.
findings: Metallic interfaces suppress rapid defect-driven degradation relative to the studied insulating supports.
Oxygen and moisture play different roles: basal-plane oxidation and accelerated defect-site corrosion are distinguished.
papers.significance: Interface selection can complement encapsulation when designing stable two-dimensional electronic devices.
papers.scope: These are material-pair-specific observations, not proof that any metal prevents oxidation or that a complete device is lifetime-qualified.
papers.source_note: Full text: Advanced Functional Materials article stored in Zotero; displayed date follows the library's journal record.

papers.headline: Balancing mobility and threshold voltage in IGZO
papers.summary: Composition and channel thickness affect more than one transistor metric at a time. A multiscale framework explains their coupled influence and identifies structural disorder as a design lever.
papers.takeaway: Reducing disorder offers a different lever from simply increasing carrier concentration.
papers.question: How can an oxide transistor combine high mobility with enhancement-mode operation when mobility and threshold voltage are coupled?
papers.approach: Machine-learning-potential molecular dynamics and DFT supply composition-dependent inputs to a transport model including structural disorder, scattering and thin-channel confinement.
findings: The model connects mobility-threshold trends across the studied compositions and thicknesses through their carrier-concentration dependence.
Changing zinc content to reduce structural disorder shifts the trade-off, rather than merely adding more carriers.
papers.significance: The framework translates atomistic material choices into device-level targets and highlights why material and geometry optimization must be considered together.
papers.scope: The results establish trends in the modeled IGZO systems, not a universally optimal composition or a complete fabrication process window.
papers.source_note: Full text: ACS Omega article stored in Zotero.

papers.headline: Growing the channel and its edge contacts together
papers.summary: Alloying-mediated phase control forms semiconducting channels and semimetallic contacts in a coordinated growth route. Clean lateral interfaces help overcome a bottleneck in p-type 2D transistors.
papers.takeaway: Contact engineering begins with how the interface is formed.
papers.question: How can reproducible, clean edge contacts be made for p-type two-dimensional channels without the oxidation and alignment problems of a separate metallization step?
papers.approach: Selective-area alloying controls the relative stability of MoTe2 phases, enabling lateral junctions between semiconducting channels and tungsten-alloyed semimetal contacts.
findings: The reported one-step edge-contact structures outperform comparison devices made with two-step metallization.
Low contact resistivity is retained over the studied short contact-length range, supported by clean interfaces and reduced gap states.
papers.significance: The work connects phase engineering and scalable synthesis to the contact challenges of compact complementary 2D electronics.
papers.scope: The reported transistors and contact-scaling tests are not a complete demonstration of a manufacturable complementary integrated circuit.
papers.source_note: Full text: Small Science article stored in the local Zotero attachment folder.

papers.headline: A better rule for designing 2D contacts
papers.summary: Work function alone does not capture every semiconductor-contact barrier. Atomistic calculations show how symmetry, contact orientation and interfacial states reshape the barrier.
papers.takeaway: Contact geometry and electronic hybridization belong in barrier predictions.
papers.question: Why do simple work-function-based predictions miss important behavior at MoS2-semimetal interfaces?
papers.approach: DFT compares type-II Weyl and Dirac semimetal contacts, then extends the Schottky-Mott picture to include interface-induced changes in vacuum levels, band edges and orbital interactions.
findings: The studied Weyl-type interfaces show contact-angle-sensitive hybridization and a downward extension of the semiconductor conduction-band edge.
Including these interfacial effects improves the reported barrier-height predictions relative to the conventional rule.
papers.significance: The analysis provides a physical basis for choosing and orienting low-resistance contacts in two-dimensional electronics.
papers.scope: This is a first-principles study of selected material interfaces. Additional experimental validation and extension to other contact systems remain necessary.
papers.source_note: Full text: ACS Nano article stored in Zotero. The library date is the journal record, not its earlier online date.

papers.headline: When a high mobility number is a geometry effect
papers.summary: Current flowing outside a transistor's nominal channel can inflate extracted mobility. Measurements, TCAD and an analytical model show how to identify and correct the geometry effect.
papers.takeaway: Reliable material comparisons require reliable mobility extraction.
papers.question: Can a transistor appear to have better carrier mobility simply because its channel island extends beyond the source and drain electrodes?
papers.approach: The study combines device measurements, TCAD and conformal-mapping-based analytical modeling to quantify fringe-current contributions.
findings: A channel island larger than the electrode-defined channel can produce an inflated field-effect mobility, with device aspect ratio affecting the error.
The proposed corrections connect the extracted value to geometry and enable more consistent comparisons.
papers.significance: Separating measurement geometry from intrinsic transport helps researchers evaluate materials and process improvements objectively.
papers.scope: The correction addresses the studied fringe-current geometry. Other extraction errors, such as contact resistance or inappropriate capacitance assumptions, still need separate checks.
papers.source_note: Full text: ACS Nano article stored in Zotero. The library's issue date is used for the recent-paper window.
